title: Napoleon's Grande Armée in Russia
intro: Napoleon set out to force the Russian Empire to comply with the continental blockade of the United Kingdom. On 24 June 1812 the multinational Grande Armée, of nearly half a million men, crossed the Neman from the Duchy of Warsaw into Russia and advanced towards Moscow.
ending: The army left Russian territory on 14 December 1812. Figures vary: Richard Riehn gives 685,000 men marching in and fewer than 70,000 known survivors, while Adam Zamoyski estimated that as many as 400,000 of 550,000 to 600,000 died, counting prisoners who died in captivity.

stops.text: Napoleon arrived near Kaunas on 23 June, and the army crossed the Neman the next day. He spent a night and the following day in Kaunas, admitting only his guards to the city.
stops.quote: On 23 June Napoleon arrived at Naugardiškė near Kaunas.

stops.text: Napoleon reached Vilnius with only light skirmishing, leaving more than 5,000 dead horses behind him. For lack of horses he had to abandon up to 100 guns and up to 500 artillery wagons.
stops.quote: Napoleon reached Vilnius on 28 June with only light skirmishing but leaving more than 5,000 dead horses in his wake.

stops.text: After the battle of Vitebsk the Russians slipped away during the night. The city and the palace of Alexander of Württemberg became Napoleon's base for the next two weeks.
stops.quote: After the battle of Vitebsk Napoleon discovered that the Russians were able to slip away during the night. The city, at the intersection of important trade routes, and the palace of Alexander of Württemberg would be Napoleon's base for the next two weeks.

stops.text: Napoleon attacked the Smolensk Kremlin in the first real confrontation of significant forces. Barclay de Tolly withdrew his troops from the burning city in the middle of the night, and the Russians left to the east.
stops.quote: The Battle of Smolensk (1812) on August 16–18 became the first real confrontation of significant forces. Napoleon surrounded the southern bank of the Dniepr, while the northern bank was guarded by Barclay's army.

stops.text: The largest battle of the invasion was fought near Borodino. The Grande Armée captured the main positions but failed to destroy the Russian army, and about a third of Napoleon's soldiers were killed or wounded.
stops.quote: The Battle of Borodino, fought on 7 September 1812, was the largest battle of the French invasion of Russia, involving more than 250,000 troops and causing at least 70,000 casualties.

stops.text: Napoleon moved into Moscow with his roughly 100,000 men and received no delegation from the city. Within 48 hours three quarters of Moscow, which had about 270,000 people before the evacuation order, was reduced to ashes by arson.
stops.quote: On 14 September 1812, Napoleon moved into Moscow. However, he was surprised to have received no delegation from the city.

stops.text: After five weeks of occupation the French Army left Moscow, still 108,000 men but with its cavalry nearly destroyed. Napoleon first took the Old Kaluga road, hoping to avoid the path his army had devastated on the way east.
stops.quote: On 19 October, after five weeks of occupation, the French Army left Moscow. Napoleon's forces still numbered 108,000 men, but his cavalry had been nearly destroyed.

stops.text: Napoleon lost the battle at Maloyaroslavets and had to return to the Smolensk road he had travelled eastward. Cossack bands under Platov, Orlov-Denisov and Davydov then attacked isolated French foraging units.
stops.quote: The Battle of Maloyaroslavets, showcasing Kutuzov's strategic maneuvering, compelled the French Army to return to the same Smolensk road they had previously traveled eastward.

stops.text: Elements of the Grande Armée were defeated at Vyazma. Starvation and disease plagued the troops, and nearly all the surviving horses died of hunger or were eaten by starving soldiers.
stops.quote: Further, defeats were inflicted on elements of the Grande Armée at Vyazma, Polotsk and Krasny.

stops.text: Short of cavalry and artillery in snow and ice, Napoleon sent the Old Guard against Miloradovich, who blocked the road to Krasny. Davout broke through, while Eugene de Beauharnais and Ney had to take a detour.
stops.quote: During the Battle of Krasnoi, Napoleon faced a critical scarcity of cavalry and artillery due to severe snowfall and icy conditions. Employing a strategic maneuver, he deployed the Old Guard against Miloradovich, who obstructed the primary road to Krasny, effectively isolating him from the main army.

stops.text: The French corps went on to Borisov, where the Russian army had destroyed the bridge over the Berezina. Two Russian armies inflicted heavy casualties on the remnants of the Grande Armée during the crossing.
stops.quote: All the French corps went on to Borisov, where a strategic bridge to cross the Berezina was destroyed by the Russian army. The crossing of the river Berezina was a final French calamity: two Russian armies inflicted heavy casualties on the remnants of the Grande Armée.

stops.text: Napoleon left the army at Smorgonie and returned to Paris by sled, leaving the sick Murat in command. Within a few days a further 20,000 people died of the cold and of diseases carried by lice.
stops.quote: On 5 December, Napoleon departed from the army at Smorgonie in a sled and returned to Paris.

stops.text: Murat and Ney took command and pressed on, leaving over 20,000 men in the hospitals of Vilnius. The remnants of the principal armies then crossed the frozen Neman and the Bug.
stops.quote: Murat and Ney assumed command, pressing forward but leaving over 20,000 men in the hospitals of Vilnius.

notes: Source is the article on the French invasion. Rivers left out as stops: the Neman crossing is placed at Kaunas (article: Napoleon arrived at Naugardiškė near Kaunas on 23 June, crossing on 24 June), and the return across the Neman (Ney recrossing on 14 December) names no town, so no final stop. Vitebsk, Maloyaroslavets, Vyazma, Krasny, Borisov and the return to Vilnius have no date in the article (the retreat stops are only placed in early November to December by context), so date and year are null. Krasny: the article also mentions a first Battle of Krasnoi on 14 August on the advance; the retreat stop follows the later Krasnoi paragraph. The Berezina text uses the article's wording that the bridge at Borisov was destroyed. Smorgonie 5 December: the article gives day and month only; 1812 is from the surrounding text (14 December 1812). Kaunas date is the arrival, not the crossing day. Wp titles for Borodino, Krasny and Smorgonie (Smarhon) and Borisov (Barysaw) are present-day names; the editor should confirm they resolve. Losses figures are attributed to Riehn and Zamoyski in the ending; the article gives other estimates (Markham, Tarle, Marshall-Cornwall, Minard's chart: 10,000 of 422,000 recrossing the Neman). Vilnius and Smolensk are in the article as supply bases; Mozhaysk, Dorogobuzh and Tarutino left out as passing mentions.
